claim: Trithorax (Trx) actively maintains the heterogeneity of neural stem cells (neuroblasts) in the developing Drosophila larval brain.
source: In this study, we report that Trithorax (Trx) actively maintains the heterogeneity of neural stem cells (neuroblasts) in the developing Drosophila larval brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that trx mutant type II neuroblasts adopt type I neuroblast identity, as demonstrated through marker expression analysis and functional assays.

claim: trx mutant type II neuroblasts gradually adopt a type I neuroblast functional identity, losing the competence to generate intermediate neural progenitors (INPs) and directly generating differentiated cells.
source: trx mutant type II neuroblasts gradually adopt a type I neuroblast functional identity, losing the competence to generate intermediate neural progenitors (INPs) and directly generating differentiated cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course clonal analysis data showing progressive changes in marker expression and progeny types in trx mutant type II neuroblasts.

claim: Trx regulates a type II neuroblast functional identity in part by maintaining chromatin in the buttonhead (btd) locus in an active state through the histone methyltransferase activity of the SET1/MLL complex.
source: Trx regulates a type II neuroblast functional identity in part by maintaining chromatin in the buttonhead (btd) locus in an active state through the histone methyltransferase activity of the SET1/MLL complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data showing Trx binding to the btd locus, H3K4 methylation patterns, and functional rescue experiments with rbbp5.

claim: btd is necessary and sufficient for eliciting a type II neuroblast functional identity.
source: Consistently, btd is necessary and sufficient for eliciting a type II neuroblast functional identity.
evidence: This claim is supported by loss-of-function experiments showing btd mutant type II neuroblasts lose INP generation capacity, and gain-of-function experiments showing btd overexpression induces type II characteristics in type I neuroblasts.

claim: Over-expression of btd restores the competence to generate INPs in trx mutant type II neuroblasts.
source: Furthermore, over-expression of btd restores the competence to generate INPs in trx mutant type II neuroblasts.
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiments showing that btd overexpression in trx mutant type II neuroblasts restores INP generation.

claim: Trx instructs a type II neuroblast functional identity by epigenetically promoting Btd expression, thereby maintaining neuroblast functional heterogeneity.
source: Thus, Trx instructs a type II neuroblast functional identity by epigenetically promoting Btd expression, thereby maintaining neuroblast functional heterogeneity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined data showing Trx binding to btd locus, H3K4 methylation, btd expression patterns, and functional rescue experiments.

claim: Neuroblasts sequentially express distinct temporal-identity transcription factors, allowing them to generate diverse differentiated cells in the fly embryonic ventral nerve cord.
source: For example, neuroblasts sequentially express distinct temporal-identity transcription factors, allowing them to generate diverse differentiated cells in the fly embryonic ventral nerve cord (Isshiki et al., 2001; Pearson and Doe, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Functionally heterogeneous stem cells directly contribute to the generation of diverse cell types during hematopoiesis, gut homeostasis, and brain development.
source: Studies in flies and vertebrate systems show that functionally heterogeneous stem cells directly contribute to the generation of diverse cell types during hematopoiesis, gut homeostasis, and brain development (Barker et al., 2007; Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008; Graf and Stadtfeld, 2008; Copley et al., 2012; Franco et al., 2012; Marianes and Spradling, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The central complex of the insect brain is comprised of an intricate network of neurons and glia that process a vast number of environmental inputs essential for daily life.
source: The central complex of the insect brain is comprised of an intricate network of neurons and glia that process a vast number of environmental inputs essential for daily life (Boyan and Reichert, 2011; Boyan and Williams, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: All differentiated cell types in the central complex arise from repeated rounds of self-renewing asymmetric divisions of type I and type II neuroblasts, which are molecularly and functionally distinct.
source: All differentiated cell types in the central complex arise from repeated rounds of self-renewing asymmetric divisions of type I and type II neuroblasts, which are molecularly and functionally distinct (Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008) (Figure1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and a figure showing the lineage structure.

claim: In every asymmetric division, a type I neuroblast always generates a precursor cell (ganglion mother cell or GMC) that divides once to produce two differentiated cells.
source: In every asymmetric division, a type I neuroblast always generates a precursor cell (ganglion mother cell or GMC) that divides once to produce two differentiated cells.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about type I neuroblast division patterns.

claim: Every asymmetric division of a type II neuroblast invariably leads to the generation of an immature INP that acquires an INP functional identity during maturation.
source: By contrast, every asymmetric division of a type II neuroblast invariably leads to the generation of an immature INP that acquires an INP functional identity during maturation.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about type II neuroblast division patterns.

claim: An INP undergoes 5–8 rounds of asymmetric division to regenerate and generate a GMC with each division.
source: An INP undergoes 5–8 rounds of asymmetric division to regenerate and generate a GMC with each division (Homem et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The ability to generate INPs functionally distinguishes type II neuroblasts from type I neuroblasts.
source: Thus, the ability to generate INPs functionally distinguishes these two types of neuroblasts.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the described division patterns of the two neuroblast types.

claim: Type II neuroblasts uniquely express the ETS transcription factor Pointed P1 (PntP1).
source: Type II neuroblasts uniquely express the ETS transcription factor Pointed P1 (PntP1) (Zhu et al., 2011; Xiao et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mis-expression of PntP1 can induce a type II neuroblast functional characteristic in a type I neuroblast.
source: Mis-expression of PntP1 can induce a type II neuroblast functional characteristic in a type I neuroblast (Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The physiological function of PntP1 in the maintenance of a type II neuroblast functional identity remains unclear.
source: However, the physiological function of PntP1 in the maintenance of a type II neuroblast functional identity remains unclear.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in knowledge identified by the authors.

claim: The pnt locus encodes at least three distinct alternatively spliced transcripts.
source: The pnt locus encodes at least three distinct alternatively spliced transcripts.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the pnt gene structure.

claim: Epigenetic mechanisms such as the methylation of histone H3 Lysine 4 (H3K4) play central roles in specifying cell type identities during development.
source: Epigenetic mechanisms such as the methylation of histone H3 Lysine 4 (H3K4) play central roles in specifying cell type identities during development (Lim et al., 2009; Ang et al., 2011; Schuettengruber et al., 2011; Shilatifard, 2012; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The evolutionarily conserved SET1/Mixed-lineage leukemia (MLL) complexes catalyze the methylation of H3K4 and maintain the target gene loci in a transcriptionally active state.
source: The evolutionarily conserved SET1/Mixed-lineage leukemia (MLL) complexes catalyze the methylation of H3K4 and maintain the target gene loci in a transcriptionally active state (Miller et al., 2001; Roguev et al., 2001; Krogan et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The fly genome encodes three orthologs of the SET1/MLL protein: Trx, Trithorax-related (Trr), and dSet1.
source: The fly genome encodes three orthologs of the SET1/MLL protein, Trx, Trithorax-related (Trr), and dSet1.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the Drosophila genome.

claim: Trx, Trr, or dSet1 can each assemble functionally active complexes by binding to Absent, small, or homeotic discs 2 (Ash2), Retinoblastoma binding protein 5 (Rbbp5), and will die slowly (Wds).
source: Similar to their mammalian counterparts, Trx, Trr, or dSet1 can each assemble functionally active complexes by binding to Absent, small, or homeotic discs 2 (Ash2), Retinoblastoma binding protein 5 (Rbbp5), and will die slowly (Wds) (Wu et al., 2008; Ardehali et al., 2011; Mohan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Trr or dSet1 regulates global mono- or tri-methylation of H3K4 respectively.
source: Functionally, Trr or dSet1 regulates global mono- or tri-methylation of H3K4 respectively.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the functions of these proteins.

claim: Trx appears to selectively regulate the expression of the Hox genes through the methylation of H3K4.
source: In contrast, Trx appears to selectively regulate the expression of the Hox genes through the methylation of H3K4 (Breen and Harte, 1993; Yu et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Little is known about the targets of Trx beyond the Hox genes.
source: However, little is known about the targets of Trx beyond the Hox genes.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in knowledge identified by the authors.

claim: Trx maintains the type II neuroblast functional identity by regulating the transcription of btd during fly larval brain neurogenesis.
source: Here, we report that Trx maintains the type II neuroblast functional identity by regulating the transcription of btd during fly larval brain neurogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including ChIP, expression analysis, and functional rescue experiments.

claim: Type II neuroblasts mutant for trx or genes encoding the core components of the SET1/MLL complex display a type I neuroblast marker expression profile and generate GMCs instead of INPs.
source: Type II neuroblasts mutant for trx or genes encoding the core components of the SET1/MLL complex display a type I neuroblast marker expression profile and generate GMCs instead of INPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing marker expression and progeny analysis in mutant clones.

claim: Trx maintains a type II neuroblast functional identity by regulating the transcription of specific target genes.
source: These results indicate that Trx maintains a type II neuroblast functional identity by regulating the transcription of specific target genes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that trx mutants show specific phenotypes without global H3K4 methylation changes.

claim: btd mutant type II neuroblasts adopt a type I neuroblast functional identity and directly generate GMCs instead of INPs.
source: btd mutant type II neuroblasts adopt a type I neuroblast functional identity and directly generate GMCs instead of INPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing marker expression and progeny analysis in btd mutant clones.

claim: Type I neuroblasts over-expressing btd assume a type II neuroblast functional identity and generate INP progeny.
source: Conversely, type I neuroblasts over-expressing btd assume a type II neuroblast functional identity and generate INP progeny.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing marker expression and progeny analysis in btd overexpression clones.

claim: Over-expression of btd restores the competence of trx mutant type II neuroblasts to generate INPs.
source: Most importantly, over-expression of btd restores the competence of trx mutant type II neuroblasts to generate INPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing rescue of INP generation in trx mutant type II neuroblasts overexpressing btd.

claim: Trx functions to epigenetically maintain Btd expression in type II neuroblasts, thereby maintaining neuroblast functional heterogeneity in the larval brain.
source: Thus, we conclude that Trx functions to epigenetically maintain Btd expression in type II neuroblasts, thereby maintaining neuroblast functional heterogeneity in the larval brain.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data showing Trx regulation of btd and btd's role in type II neuroblast identity.

claim: trx mutant type I neuroblasts maintained the expression of Deadpan (Dpn) and Asense (Ase) and the cytoplasmic localization of Prospero (Pros), but lacked PntP1 expression.
source: Identical to wild-type neuroblasts, trx mutant type I neuroblasts maintained the expression of Deadpan (Dpn) and Asense (Ase) and the cytoplasmic localization of Prospero (Pros), but lacked PntP1 expression (Dpn+Ase+PntP1−Proscytoplasmic) (Table 1, data not presented).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on marker expression in trx mutant type I neuroblasts.

claim: Both wild-type and trx mutant type I neuroblasts were always surrounded by GMCs.
source: In addition, both wild-type and trx mutant type I neuroblasts were always surrounded by GMCs (Dpn−Ase+Prosnuclear) (data not presented).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on progeny analysis.

claim: Trx is dispensable for the maintenance of a type I neuroblast functional identity.
source: Thus, Trx is dispensable for the maintenance of a type I neuroblast functional identity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that trx mutant type I neuroblasts maintain normal identity and function.

claim: All wild-type type II neuroblasts displayed a Dpn+Ase−PntP1+Pros− marker expression profile in all stages examined.
source: While all wild-type type II neuroblasts displayed a Dpn+Ase−PntP1+Pros− marker expression profile in all stages examined, trx mutant type II neuroblasts progressively altered their marker expression profile (Figure 1A–D, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and table.

claim: trx mutant type II neuroblasts progressively altered their marker expression profile.
source: While all wild-type type II neuroblasts displayed a Dpn+Ase−PntP1+Pros− marker expression profile in all stages examined, trx mutant type II neuroblasts progressively altered their marker expression profile (Figure 1A–D, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and table.

claim: Almost all trx mutant type II neuroblasts in 72-hr clones displayed a type I neuroblast marker expression profile.
source: Strikingly, almost all trx mutant type II neuroblasts in 72-hr clones displayed a type I neuroblast marker expression profile (Figure 1B–D; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and table.

claim: trx mutant type II neuroblasts adopt a type I neuroblast identity.
source: These data strongly suggest that trx mutant type II neuroblasts adopt a type I neuroblast identity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the marker expression data.

claim: A control type II neuroblast at 72 hr after clone induction was surrounded by approximately 20 INPs and 12 INP-derived GMCs that can be unambiguously identified by the expression of an erm-lacZ reporter transgene.
source: At 72 hr after clone induction, a control type II neuroblast was surrounded by approximately 20 INPs and 12 INP-derived GMCs that can be unambiguously identified by the expression of an erm-lacZ reporter transgene (Figure 1C,E–F,H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: An identically staged trx mutant neuroblast was directly surrounded by non-neuroblast progeny that displayed a Dpn−Ase+Prosnuclearerm-lacZ− expression profile identical to GMCs derived from type I neuroblasts.
source: In contrast, an identically staged trx mutant neuroblast was directly surrounded by non-neuroblast progeny that displayed a Dpn−Ase+Prosnuclearerm-lacZ− expression profile identical to GMCs derived from type I neuroblasts (Figure 1C,G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: trx mutant clones contained an average of 3 INPs and 4 INP-derived GMCs located at the extreme distal end of the clone.
source: Although trx mutant clones also contained an average of 3 INPs and 4 INP-derived GMCs, these cells were located at the extreme distal end of the clone, consistent with trx mutant type II neuroblasts adopting a type I neuroblast identity following the clone induction (Figure 1C,E,G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Trx regulates neuroblast heterogeneity by maintaining a type II neuroblast identity.
source: These data strongly suggest that Trx regulates neuroblast heterogeneity by maintaining a type II neuroblast identity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data on trx mutant phenotypes.

claim: The competence to generate INPs is a main feature that distinguishes the functional identity of a type II neuroblast from that of a type I neuroblast.
source: The competence to generate INPs is a main feature that distinguishes the functional identity of a type II neuroblast from that of a type I neuroblast (Weng and Lee, 2011; Homem and Knoblich, 2012; Janssens and Lee, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: brain tumor (brat) and erm function in the immature INP to promote INP identity specification in the type II neuroblast lineage.
source: brain tumor (brat) and erm function in the immature INP to promote INP identity specification in the type II neuroblast lineage, and the defective specification of an INP identity leads to the formation of supernumerary type II neuroblasts in the brat or erm mutant brain (Xiao et al., 2012; Eroglu et al., 2014; Janssens et al., 2014; Koe et al., 2014; Komori et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The defective specification of an INP identity leads to the formation of supernumerary type II neuroblasts in the brat or erm mutant brain.
source: brain tumor (brat) and erm function in the immature INP to promote INP identity specification in the type II neuroblast lineage, and the defective specification of an INP identity leads to the formation of supernumerary type II neuroblasts in the brat or erm mutant brain (Xiao et al., 2012; Eroglu et al., 2014; Janssens et al., 2014; Koe et al., 2014; Komori et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: If trx mutant type II neuroblasts adopt a type I neuroblast functional identity, their progeny should be insensitive to the loss of brat or erm function and generate differentiated cells instead of reverting into supernumerary neuroblasts.
source: If trx mutant type II neuroblasts indeed adopt a type I neuroblast functional identity, their progeny should be insensitive to the loss of brat or erm function and generate differentiated cells instead of reverting into supernumerary neuroblasts.
evidence: This claim represents a hypothesis based on logical inference from known functions of brat and erm.

claim: A control type II neuroblast clone in the brat mutant brain contained more than 100 supernumerary type II neuroblasts and was devoid of GMCs and neurons.
source: A control type II neuroblast clone in the brat mutant brain contained more than 100 supernumerary type II neuroblasts and was devoid of GMCs and neurons (Figure 2A,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: A trx mutant type II neuroblast clone in the brat mutant brain contained far fewer supernumerary type II neuroblasts and far more GMCs and neurons as compared to the control clone.
source: By contrast, a trx mutant type II neuroblast clone in the brat mutant brain contained far fewer supernumerary type II neuroblasts and far more GMCs and neurons as compared to the control clone (Figure 2A–B,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: A control type II neuroblast clone in the erm mutant brain contained more than 50 supernumerary type II neuroblasts and few GMCs and neurons.
source: Similarly, a control type II neuroblast clone in the erm mutant brain contained more than 50 supernumerary type II neuroblasts and few GMCs and neurons (Figure 2C,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: A trx mutant type II neuroblast clone in the erm mutant brain contained fewer supernumerary type II neuroblasts but more GMCs and neurons as compared to the control clone.
source: In contrast, a trx mutant type II neuroblast clone in the erm mutant brain contained fewer supernumerary type II neuroblasts but more GMCs and neurons as compared to the control clone (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: trx mutant type II neuroblasts lost the competence to generate immature INPs.
source: Together, these data strongly suggest that trx mutant type II neuroblasts lost the competence to generate immature INPs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the genetic interaction data with brat and erm mutants.

claim: Pros segregates exclusively into GMCs where it suppresses a type I neuroblast functional identity during asymmetric division of a type I neuroblast.
source: Pros segregates exclusively into GMCs where it suppresses a type I neuroblast functional identity during asymmetric division of a type I neuroblast, but is undetectable in mitotic type II neuroblasts (Knoblich et al., 1995; Spana and Doe, 1995; Choksi et al., 2006; Bayraktar et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pros is undetectable in mitotic type II neuroblasts.
source: Pros segregates exclusively into GMCs where it suppresses a type I neuroblast functional identity during asymmetric division of a type I neuroblast, but is undetectable in mitotic type II neuroblasts (Knoblich et al., 1995; Spana and Doe, 1995; Choksi et al., 2006; Bayraktar et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In a telophase trx mutant type II neuroblast, Pros localized asymmetrically in the basal cortex and segregated uniquely into the cortex of the future non-neuroblast progeny.
source: In a telophase trx mutant type II neuroblast, however, Pros localized asymmetrically in the basal cortex and segregated uniquely into the cortex of the future non-neuroblast progeny (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Removing pros function in trx mutant type II neuroblasts leads to the formation of supernumerary type I neuroblasts.
source: Most importantly, removing pros function in trx mutant type II neuroblasts leads to the formation of supernumerary type I neuroblasts (Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: trx mutant type II neuroblasts adopt a type I neuroblast functional identity and directly generate GMCs.
source: These data confirm that trx mutant type II neuroblasts adopt a type I neuroblast functional identity and directly generate GMCs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the Pros localization and pros mutant data.

claim: trx regulates neuroblast heterogeneity by maintaining a type II neuroblast functional identity.
source: Thus, we conclude that trx regulates neuroblast heterogeneity by maintaining a type II neuroblast functional identity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data.

claim: The histone methylation activity of Trx is required for maintaining a type II neuroblast functional identity.
source: We assessed whether the histone methylation activity of Trx is required for maintaining a type II neuroblast functional identity.
evidence: This claim represents a hypothesis tested by the authors.

claim: The trxZ11 allele results in a missense mutation in the SET domain of Trx and reduces the histone methyltransferase activity of the Trx protein.
source: We induced mosaic clones derived from type II neuroblasts carrying the trxZ11 allele, which results in a missense mutation in the SET domain of Trx and reduces the histone methyltransferase activity of the Trx protein (Smith et al., 2004; Tie et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Twenty-seven percent of trxZ11 type II neuroblasts assumed a type I neuroblast functional identity as determined by both the expression of a type I neuroblast marker expression profile and the generation of GMCs.
source: Twenty-seven percent of trxZ11 type II neuroblasts assumed a type I neuroblast functional identity as determined by both the expression of a type I neuroblast marker expression profile and the generation of GMCs (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The histone methylation activity of Trx is essential for the maintenance of a type II neuroblast functional identity.
source: This result indicates that the histone methylation activity of Trx is essential for the maintenance of a type II neuroblast functional identity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the trxZ11 mutant data.

claim: Trx was co-purified with the core components of the SET1/MLL complex, Ash2, Rbbp5, and Wds, from the lysate extracted from S2 cells.
source: Trx was co-purified with the core components of the SET1/MLL complex, Ash2, Rbbp5, and Wds, from the lysate extracted from S2 cells (Mohan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Knocking down the function of ash2, rbbp5, or wds individually leads to fewer type II neuroblasts and INPs per brain lobe, identical to reducing trx function.
source: Indeed, knocking down the function of ash2, rbbp5, or wds individually leads to fewer type II neuroblasts and INPs per brain lobe, identical to reducing trx function (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Trx maintains a type II neuroblast functional identity through the SET1/MLL complex via a mechanism dependent of the histone methyltransferase activity.
source: Together, these data strongly support our hypothesis that Trx maintains a type II neuroblast functional identity through the SET1/MLL complex via a mechanism dependent of the histone methyltransferase activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined data on trx, ash2, rbbp5, and wds.

claim: Rbbp5 is essential for eliciting the histone methyltransferase activity of the SET1/MLL complex.
source: We focus on the Rbbp5 protein, which is essential for eliciting the histone methyltransferase activity of the SET1/MLL complex (Cao et al., 2010), to test whether Trx maintains a type II neuroblast functional identity through the SET1/MLL complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: rbbp5null type II neuroblasts adopt a type I neuroblast functional identity.
source: Mutant analyses confirmed that rbbp5null type II neuroblasts indeed adopt a type I neuroblast functional identity (Figure 3C–F, Table 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and table.

claim: A rbbp5null type II neuroblast is phenotypically indistinguishable from a trx mutant type II neuroblast.
source: Thus, a rbbp5null type II neuroblast is phenotypically indistinguishable from a trx mutant type II neuroblast.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing the phenotypes of rbbp5null and trx mutant type II neuroblasts.

claim: All cells in the clones derived from single rbbp5null type II neuroblast showed undetectable mono- and tri-methylation of H3K4.
source: We next examined the H3K4 methylation pattern in the rbbp5null type II neuroblast. All cells in the clones derived from single rbbp5null type II neuroblast showed undetectable mono- and tri-methylation of H3K4 (Figure 3G, data not presented).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The SET1/MLL complex exerts its regulatory functions through the H3K4 methylation.
source: This result is consistent with the SET1/MLL complex exerting its regulatory functions through the H3K4 methylation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the H3K4 methylation data in rbbp5null mutants.

claim: Over-expression of a UAS-rbbp5FL transgene that encodes a full-length Rbbp5 completely restored a type II neuroblast functional identity and significantly restored both the H3K4 mono- and tri-methylation in rbbp5null type II neuroblasts.
source: Most importantly, over-expression of a UAS-rbbp5FL transgene that encodes a full-length Rbbp5 completely restored a type II neuroblast functional identity and significantly restored both the H3K4 mono- and tri-methylation in rbbp5null type II neuroblasts (Figure 3F,H–I, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, data not presented).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Over-expression of a UAS-rbbp5SG transgene, which encodes a mutant Rbbp5 protein predicted to perturb the histone methyltransferase activity of the SET1/MLL complex, failed to restore a type II neuroblast functional identity and the methylation of H3K4 in rbbp5null type II neuroblasts.
source: By contrast, over-expression of a UAS-rbbp5SG transgene, which encodes a mutant Rbbp5 protein predicted to perturb the histone methyltransferase activity of the SET1/MLL complex (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) (Cao et al., 2010), failed to restore a type II neuroblast functional identity and the methylation of H3K4 in rbbp5null type II neuroblasts (Figure 3F,J–K, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, data not presented).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and a citation.

claim: Type II neuroblasts bearing a strong ash2 mutant allele adopted a type I neuroblast functional identity and lost most H3K4 methylation.
source: Similarly, type II neuroblasts bearing a strong ash2 mutant allele also adopted a type I neuroblast functional identity and lost most H3K4 methylation based on the same criteria (data not presented).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data (not shown in manuscript).

claim: The histone methyltransferase activity of the SET1/MLL complex is required for the maintenance of a type II neuroblast identity.
source: Thus, the histone methyltransferase activity of the SET1/MLL complex is required for the maintenance of a type II neuroblast identity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined data on rbbp5 and ash2 mutants and rescue experiments.

claim: Trx maintains a functional identity of type II neuroblasts through the histone methylation activity of the SET1/MLL complex.
source: We conclude that Trx maintains a functional identity of type II neuroblasts through the histone methylation activity of the SET1/MLL complex.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data.

claim: Knocking down the function of trr or dset1 drastically reduced the global H3K4 mono- or tri-methylation in type II neuroblasts but had no effects on the maintenance of their functional identity.
source: Knocking down the function of trr or dset1 drastically reduced the global H3K4 mono- or tri-methylation in type II neuroblasts but had no effects on the maintenance of their functional identity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Removing trx function had no appreciable effects on the global H3K4 pattern in type II neuroblasts.
source: By contrast, removing trx function had no appreciable effects on the global H3K4 pattern in type II neuroblasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K–N).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Trx maintains the type II neuroblast functional identity by regulating a small number of genes that are specifically expressed in the type II neuroblast.
source: These data led us to hypothesize that Trx maintains the type II neuroblast functional identity by regulating a small number of genes that are specifically expressed in the type II neuroblast.
evidence: This claim represents a hypothesis based on inference from the H3K4 methylation data.

claim: pnt and btd were among a small number of genes that were dramatically up-regulated in the mRNAs isolated from larval brains enriched with type II neuroblasts as compared to the mRNAs isolated from larval brains enriched with type I neuroblasts.
source: pnt and btd were among a small number of genes that were dramatically up-regulated in the mRNAs isolated from larval brains enriched with type II neuroblasts as compared to the mRNAs isolated from larval brains enriched with type I neuroblasts.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression profiling data.

claim: Both pntP1 and btd transcripts were highly enriched in the brain lysate enriched with type II neuroblasts by qRT-PCR.
source: We confirmed that both pntP1 and btd transcripts were indeed highly enriched in the brain lysate enriched with type II neuroblasts by qRT-PCR (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Trx binds to the transcription start site for both the pntP1 and btd transcription units.
source: Furthermore, we detected the binding of Trx to the transcription start site for both the pntP1 and btd transcription units (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data shown in figures.

claim: The promoter region of both the pntP1 and btd transcription units displayed a high level of H3K4 di-methylation.
source: In addition, the promoter region of both the pntP1 and btd transcription units also displayed a high level of H3K4 di-methylation, consistent with Trx-maintaining chromatin in an active state in these two loci through the H3K4 methylation (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data shown in figures.

claim: Trx did not bind to the negative control region located 7.5 kilobases 3ʹ from the btd transcription unit.
source: By contrast, we did not detect Trx binding to the negative control region located 7.5 kilobases 3ʹ from the btd transcription unit (Figure 4B; data not presented) (Petruk et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data shown in figures and a citation.

claim: Both pnt and btd are the direct target genes of Trx.
source: Thus, both pnt and btd are the direct target genes of Trx.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the ChIP data showing Trx binding and H3K4 methylation at these loci.

claim: An enhancer element from the btd gene is sufficient to induce type II neuroblast-specific expression of a UAS-mCD8::gfp reporter transgene in wild-type brain.
source: The expression of a UAS reporter transgene driven by btd-Gal4 was detected specifically in type II neuroblasts but was undetectable in type I neuroblasts in wild-type brains (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The expression of btd-Gal4 was drastically reduced in rbbp5null mutant brains.
source: Importantly, the expression of btd-Gal4 was drastically reduced in rbbp5null mutant brains (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: btd is an excellent candidate for functioning downstream of trx to maintain the type II neuroblast functional identity.
source: Together, these data strongly support our hypothesis that btd is an excellent candidate for functioning downstream of trx to maintain the type II neuroblast functional identity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined data on btd expression, Trx binding, and regulation by rbbp5.

claim: btd mutant type II neuroblasts maintained a type II neuroblast marker expression profile in all stages examined.
source: btd mutant type II neuroblasts maintained a type II neuroblast marker expression profile in all stages examined, but these clones displayed a time-dependent reduction in INPs (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: btd mutant type II neuroblast clones displayed a time-dependent reduction in INPs.
source: btd mutant type II neuroblasts maintained a type II neuroblast marker expression profile in all stages examined, but these clones displayed a time-dependent reduction in INPs (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: INPs in the 72-hr btd mutant clone were always located at the extreme distal end of the clone.
source: Unlike the control clone, however, INPs in the 72-hr btd mutant clone were always located at the extreme distal end of the clone (data not presented).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data (not shown in manuscript).

claim: btd mutant type II neuroblasts were surrounded by 1–2 progeny resembling Ase− immature INPs but never Ase+ immature INPs.
source: In these clones, btd mutant type II neuroblasts were surrounded by 1–2 progeny resembling Ase− immature INPs but never Ase+ immature INPs (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The remaining cells directly adjacent to the btd mutant type II neuroblast displayed a marker expression profile indicative of GMCs and immature neurons that are normally found in the type I neuroblast lineage.
source: Instead, the remaining cells directly adjacent to the btd mutant type II neuroblast displayed a marker expression profile indicative of GMCs and immature neurons that are normally found in the type I neuroblast lineage (Figure 4F,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Supernumerary neuroblast formation was never detected in the btd, brat double type II neuroblast clone.
source: Most importantly, we never detected supernumerary neuroblast formation in the btd, brat double type II neuroblast clone, indicating that the direct progeny of the btd mutant type II neuroblast were insensitive to the loss of brat function (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The direct progeny of the btd mutant type II neuroblast were insensitive to the loss of brat function.
source: Most importantly, we never detected supernumerary neuroblast formation in the btd, brat double type II neuroblast clone, indicating that the direct progeny of the btd mutant type II neuroblast were insensitive to the loss of brat function (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: btd mutant type II neuroblasts generate non-functional Ase− immature INPs that likely adopt an identity of GMCs normally found in the type I neuroblast lineage.
source: These data led us to conclude that btd mutant type II neuroblasts generate non-functional Ase− immature INPs that likely adopt an identity of GMCs normally found in the type I neuroblast lineage.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the marker expression and brat interaction data.

claim: Trx most likely maintains the type II neuroblast functional identity through btd.
source: Thus, we conclude that Trx most likely maintains the type II neuroblast functional identity through btd.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined data on btd function and regulation by Trx.

claim: Eighteen percent of type I neuroblasts mis-expressing btd lost Ase expression and generated progeny displaying a marker expression profile that is typically diagnostic of an immature INP or an INP.
source: Eighteen percent of type I neuroblasts mis-expressing btd lost Ase expression and generated progeny displaying a marker expression profile that is typically diagnostic of an immature INP or an INP (Figure 5B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Another 10% of type I neuroblasts mis-expressing btd generated progeny that resembled immature INPs or INPs by marker expression, but maintained Ase expression.
source: Another 10% of type I neuroblasts mis-expressing btd generated progeny that resembled immature INPs or INPs by marker expression, but maintained Ase expression (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Mis-expression of btd is sufficient to trigger the characteristics that are specific for a type II neuroblast in a type I neuroblast.
source: Thus, we conclude that mis-expression of btd is sufficient to trigger the characteristics that are specific for a type II neuroblast in a type I neuroblast.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the btd overexpression data in type I neuroblasts.

claim: Removing brat function had no effects on the identities of progeny derived from control type I neuroblasts.
source: While removing brat function had no effects on the identities of progeny derived from control type I neuroblasts, it led to supernumerary type II neuroblast formation in the lineage clones derived from single type I neuroblasts mis-expressing btd (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Removing brat function led to supernumerary type II neuroblast formation in the lineage clones derived from single type I neuroblasts mis-expressing btd.
source: While removing brat function had no effects on the identities of progeny derived from control type I neuroblasts, it led to supernumerary type II neuroblast formation in the lineage clones derived from single type I neuroblasts mis-expressing btd (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Removing erm function led to supernumerary type II neuroblast formation in the lineage clones derived from single type I neuroblast mis-expressing btd.
source: Similarly, removing erm function also led to supernumerary type II neuroblast formation in the lineage clones derived from single type I neuroblast mis-expressing btd while not having any effects on the control type I neuroblast clones (Figure 5G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Removing erm function had no effects on control type I neuroblast clones.
source: Similarly, removing erm function also led to supernumerary type II neuroblast formation in the lineage clones derived from single type I neuroblast mis-expressing btd while not having any effects on the control type I neuroblast clones (Figure 5G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: brat and erm function specifically in the immature INP to promote an INP identity.
source: Since brat and erm function specifically in the immature INP to promote an INP identity (Xiao et al., 2012; Janssens et al., 2014; Komori et al., 2014), these data strongly suggest that mis-expression of btd was sufficient to endow a type I neuroblast with the competence to generate INPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mis-expression of btd was sufficient to endow a type I neuroblast with the competence to generate INPs.
source: Since brat and erm function specifically in the immature INP to promote an INP identity (Xiao et al., 2012; Janssens et al., 2014; Komori et al., 2014), these data strongly suggest that mis-expression of btd was sufficient to endow a type I neuroblast with the competence to generate INPs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the genetic interaction data with brat and erm.

claim: btd plays an important role in eliciting the functional identity of a type II neuroblast.
source: Thus, we conclude that btd plays an important role in eliciting the functional identity of a type II neuroblast.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined loss-of-function and gain-of-function data for btd.

claim: 40% of trx mutant type II neuroblasts over-expressing btd regained the characteristics that are specific for a type II neuroblast including loss of Ase expression and the generation of immature INPs and INPs.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, 40% of trx mutant type II over-expressing btd regained the characteristics that are specific for a type II neuroblast including loss of Ase expression and the generation of immature INPs and INPs (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Over-expression of btd significantly enabled trx mutant type II neuroblasts to generate INPs.
source: Furthermore, over-expression of btd also significantly enabled trx mutant type II neuroblasts to generate INPs (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: btd is a key downstream target gene of Trx in the maintenance of the type II neuroblast functional identity.
source: Thus, we conclude that btd is a key downstream target gene of Trx in the maintenance of the type II neuroblast functional identity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the rescue experiments showing btd overexpression restores type II identity in trx mutants.

claim: Maintaining functionally distinct stem cell populations allows higher organisms to generate the requisite number of diverse cell types required for organogenesis.
source: Maintaining functionally distinct stem cell populations allows higher organisms to generate the requisite number of diverse cell types required for organogenesis.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in developmental biology.

claim: Neural stem cells in the subventricular zone and in the outer subventricular zone collectively contribute to the generation of all the cell types required for the development of a human brain.
source: For example, neural stem cells in the subventricular zone and in the outer subventricular zone collectively contribute to the generation of all the cell types required for the development of a human brain (Fietz et al., 2010; Hansen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Heterogeneous stem cell pools have been reported in other organs including the blood and intestine.
source: Similarly, heterogeneous stem cell pools have also been reported in other organs including the blood and intestine (Barker et al., 2007; Graf and Stadtfeld, 2008; Copley et al., 2012; Marianes and Spradling, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The mechanisms that maintain the functional heterogeneity of stem cells have never been reported.
source: Although the mechanisms that specify the identity of distinct stem cell types within a given organ have been proposed, the mechanisms that maintain the functional heterogeneity of stem cells have never been reported.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in knowledge identified by the authors.

claim: Trx functions uniquely to maintain a type II neuroblast identity through the H3K4 methylation activity of the SET1/MLL complex, thereby contributing to neuroblast heterogeneity during larval brain neurogenesis.
source: We discovered that Trx functions uniquely to maintain a type II neuroblast identity through the H3K4 methylation activity of the SET1/MLL complex, thereby contributing to neuroblast heterogeneity during larval brain neurogenesis.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The Trx-Btd-dependent mechanism provides the first mechanistic insight into the maintenance of stem cell functional heterogeneity within an organ.
source: To our knowledge, this Trx-Btd-dependent mechanism provides the first mechanistic insight into the maintenance of stem cell functional heterogeneity within an organ (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the novelty of the findings in the context of existing literature.

claim: The homologs of Trx and Btd have been shown to play critical roles in regulating vertebrate neural stem cell functions.
source: The homologs of Trx and Btd have been shown to play critical roles in regulating vertebrate neural stem cell functions (Lim et al., 2009; MuhChyi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The SET1/MLL histone methyltransferase complex might also contribute to the maintenance of stem cell heterogeneity in other higher eukaryotes.
source: Our findings lead us to speculate that the SET1/MLL histone methyltransferase complex might also contribute to the maintenance of stem cell heterogeneity in other higher eukaryotes.
evidence: This claim represents speculation based on the findings and conservation of the mechanisms.

claim: The core components of the SET1/MLL complex is required for the maintenance of the H3K4 methylation in a type II neuroblast and the maintenance of a type II neuroblast functional identity.
source: Our data showed that the core components of the SET1/MLL complex is required for the maintenance of the H3K4 methylation in a type II neuroblast and the maintenance of a type II neuroblast functional identity (Figure 3C–D,F, Figure 3—figure supplement1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Over-expression of rbbp5FL, but not rbbp5SG, restored both H3K4 methylation and a type II neuroblast functional identity in rbbp5 null type II neuroblasts.
source: Most importantly, over-expression of rbbp5FL, but not rbbp5SG, which encodes a mutant Rbbp5 protein that partially compromises the H3K4 methylation activity of the SET1/MLL complex (Cao et al., 2010), restored both H3K4 methylation and a type II neuroblast functional identity in rbbp5 null type II neuroblasts (Figure 3C–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and a citation.

claim: The H3K4 methylation activity of the SET1/MLL complex is required for maintaining the functional identity of a type II neuroblast.
source: These results indicate that the H3K4 methylation activity of the SET1/MLL complex is required for maintaining the functional identity of a type II neuroblast.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the rbbp5 rescue experiments.

claim: Removing trx function did not alter the global H3K4 methylation.
source: Although the methylation activity of Trx was required for maintaining the type II neuroblast functional identity, removing trx function did not alter the global H3K4 methylation (Figure 3A–B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1K–N).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Knocking down the function of trr or dset1 did not affect the maintenance of a type II neuroblast functional identity despite resulting in the global loss of H3K4 mono- or tri-methylation.
source: In contrast, knocking down the function of trr or dset1 did not affect the maintenance of a type II neuroblast functional identity despite resulting in the global loss of H3K4 mono- or tri-methylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Trx maintains a type II neuroblast functional identity by regulating H3K4 methylation in specific downstream target loci.
source: These data strongly suggest that Trx maintains a type II neuroblast functional identity by regulating H3K4 methylation in specific downstream target loci.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the differential effects of trx, trr, and dset1 on global vs. specific H3K4 methylation.

claim: The functional identity of a type II neuroblast is defined by the competence of a neuroblast to generate INPs.
source: The functional identity of a type II neuroblast is defined by the competence of a neuroblast to generate INPs (Weng and Lee, 2011; Homem and Knoblich, 2012; Janssens and Lee, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Trx plays a central role in maintaining the functional identity of a type II neuroblast by promoting the expression of a small number of genes.
source: Our data indicate Trx plays a central role in maintaining the functional identity of a type II neuroblast by promoting the expression of a small number of genes (Figures 1 and 4A).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: btd encodes a C2H2 zinc finger transcription factor required for proper patterning of the head segment during fly embryogenesis and likely functions as a transcription activator.
source: btd encodes a C2H2 zinc finger transcription factor required for proper patterning of the head segment during fly embryogenesis and likely functions as a transcription activator (Wimmer et al., 1993; Schöck et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The role of Btd in regulating neuroblasts has never been established.
source: However, the role of Btd in regulating neuroblasts has never been established, and the mechanisms by which Btd elicits biological responses remain unclear.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in knowledge identified by the authors.

claim: The mechanisms by which Btd elicits biological responses remain unclear.
source: However, the role of Btd in regulating neuroblasts has never been established, and the mechanisms by which Btd elicits biological responses remain unclear.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in knowledge identified by the authors.

claim: Certain co-factors might be required for Btd to efficiently activate its target gene transcription, and a lower abundance of these co-factors in type I neuroblasts hinders the functional output of mis-expressed Btd.
source: First, certain co-factors might be required for Btd to efficiently activate its target gene transcription, and a lower abundance of these co-factors in type I neuroblasts hinders the functional output of mis-expressed Btd.
evidence: This claim represents speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: The epigenetic landscape might be vastly different between the two types of neuroblasts such that mis-expressed Btd may not have access to all of its target genes required to elicit the type II neuroblast functional identity in a type I neuroblast.
source: Second, the epigenetic landscape might be vastly different between the two types of neuroblasts such that mis-expressed Btd may not have access to all of its target genes required to elicit the type II neuroblast functional identity in a type I neuroblast.
evidence: This claim represents speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: Additional transcription factors might function in parallel with Btd to regulate the functional identity of a type II neuroblast.
source: Lastly, additional transcription factors might function in parallel with Btd to regulate the functional identity of a type II neuroblast.
evidence: This claim represents speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: Btd is a highly conserved transcription factor.
source: Btd is a highly conserved transcription factor (Estella and Mann, 2010; MuhChyi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Future studies to elucidate the mechanisms by which Btd regulates the functional identity of a type II neuroblast will provide critical insight in the regulation of neural stem cell heterogeneity during both invertebrate as well as vertebrate neurogenesis.
source: Future studies to elucidate the mechanisms by which Btd regulates the functional identity of a type II neuroblast will provide critical insight in the regulation of neural stem cell heterogeneity during both invertebrate as well as vertebrate neurogenesis.
evidence: This claim represents speculation about the implications of future research.

claim: Knocking down the function of the pnt gene had no effect on the maintenance of the type II neuroblast functional identity.
source: Unexpectedly, knocking down the function of the pnt gene, which encodes at least three alternatively spliced transcripts, had no effect on the maintenance of the type II neuroblast functional identity, and instead, resulted in the formation of supernumerary type II neuroblasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Knocking down the function of the pnt gene resulted in the formation of supernumerary type II neuroblasts.
source: Unexpectedly, knocking down the function of the pnt gene, which encodes at least three alternatively spliced transcripts, had no effect on the maintenance of the type II neuroblast functional identity, and instead, resulted in the formation of supernumerary type II neuroblasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Pnt functions in the immature INP to specify an INP identity.
source: This result led us to revise our hypothesis and propose that Pnt functions in the immature INP to specify an INP identity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the pnt knockdown phenotype.

claim: Heterozygosity of the pnt locus dominantly enhanced the supernumerary neuroblast in the brat or erm hypomorphic genetic background.
source: Consistently, heterozygosity of the pnt locus dominantly enhanced the supernumerary neuroblast in the brat or erm hypomorphic genetic background (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Over-expression of pntP1 failed to restore the functional identity of a type II neuroblast in trx mutant type II neuroblasts.
source: Furthermore, over-expression of pntP1 failed to restore the functional identity of a type II neuroblast in trx mutant type II neuroblasts (data not presented).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data (not shown in manuscript).

claim: pnt mainly functions to specify an INP identity rather than to maintain the type II neuroblast functional identity.
source: Together, these data strongly suggest that pnt mainly functions to specify an INP identity rather than to maintain the type II neuroblast functional identity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined data on pnt function.

claim: In addition to maintaining the type II neuroblast functional identity, Trx also functions to promote INP identity specification through pnt.
source: Thus, we propose that in addition to maintaining the type II neuroblast functional identity, Trx also functions to promote INP identity specification through pnt (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined data on Trx regulation of pnt and pnt function.

claim: Strategies that uniquely target the functional properties of cancer stem cells will revolutionize cancer treatments.
source: Strategies that uniquely target the functional properties of cancer stem cells will revolutionize cancer treatments.
evidence: This claim represents speculation about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: Cancer stem cells generate a hierarchy of progeny that include cell types directly contributing to the exponential expansion of cancer stem cells.
source: Cancer stem cells generate a hierarchy of progeny that include cell types directly contributing to the exponential expansion of cancer stem cells (Magee et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Reprogramming the functional identity of cancer stem cells to bypass the cell types that directly contribute to the exponential expansion of cancer stem cells should halt further tumor growth.
source: Thus, reprogramming their functional identity to bypass the cell types that directly contribute to the exponential expansion of cancer stem cells should halt further tumor growth.
evidence: This claim represents speculation based on logical inference.

claim: Removing trx function efficiently reduced the number of supernumerary type II neuroblasts and increased the number of differentiated cells in the brat or erm mutant brain.
source: In our study, removing trx function efficiently reduced the number of supernumerary type II neuroblasts, which are proposed to serve as cancer stem cells in several Drosophila brain tumor models (Caussinus and Gonzalez, 2005; Xiao et al., 2012; Eroglu et al., 2014; Janssens et al., 2014; Koe et al., 2014; Komori et al., 2014), and increased the number of differentiated cells in the brat or erm mutant brain (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and citations.

claim: Supernumerary type II neuroblasts are proposed to serve as cancer stem cells in several Drosophila brain tumor models.
source: In our study, removing trx function efficiently reduced the number of supernumerary type II neuroblasts, which are proposed to serve as cancer stem cells in several Drosophila brain tumor models (Caussinus and Gonzalez, 2005; Xiao et al., 2012; Eroglu et al., 2014; Janssens et al., 2014; Koe et al., 2014; Komori et al., 2014), and increased the number of differentiated cells in the brat or erm mutant brain (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Attenuating the competence of type II neuroblasts to generate INPs by removing btd function efficiently halted the expansion of brat or erm mutant brain tumors.
source: Similarly, attenuating the competence of type II neuroblasts to generate INPs by removing btd function also efficiently halted the expansion of brat or erm mutant brain tumors (Figure 4I–J, data not presented).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and additional data not shown.

claim: Reprogramming the functional identity of putative cancer stem cells can significantly alter the course of tumorigenesis.
source: Our results strongly support the hypothesis that reprogramming the functional identity of putative cancer stem cells can significantly alter the course of tumorigenesis.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results in tumor models.

claim: Understanding the mechanisms that maintain stem cell heterogeneity during normal development might provide novel insight into designing rational therapies to promote switching of cancer stem cells to an alternative, non-cancerous stem cell type.
source: As such, understanding the mechanisms that maintain stem cell heterogeneity during normal development might provide novel insight into designing rational therapies to promote switching of cancer stem cells to an alternative, non-cancerous stem cell type.
evidence: This claim represents speculation about potential therapeutic applications based on the findings.
